title: Android TV Box Bought From Amazon Comes Pre-Installed With Malware
content:
#### Description
Recently, systems security consultant Daniel Milisic discovered that an Android TV box purchased from Amazon was pre-loaded with persistent, sophisticated malware baked into its firmware. The T95 streaming device uses an Android 10-based ROM signed with test keys and the ADB (Android Debug Bridge) open over Ethernet and WiFi. This is a suspicious configuration as ADB can be used to connect to devices for unrestricted filesystem access, command execution, software installation, data modification, and remote control. 

While analyzing the DNS request in Pi-hole, Milisic discovered that the device was attempting to connect to several IP addresses associated with active malware.  Milisic believes the malware installed on the device is a strain that resembles 'CopyCat,' a sophisticated Android malware first discovered by Check Point in 2017. This malware was previously seen in an adware campaign where it infected 14 million Android devices to make its operators over $1,500,000 in profits.

#### Reference URL(s)
1. https://www.malwarebytes.com/blog/news/2023/01/preinstalled-malware-infested-t95-tv-box-from-amazon
2. https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/android-tv-box-on-amazon-came-pre-installed-with-malware/
3. https://github.com/DesktopECHO/T95-H616-Malware

#### Publication Date
January 30, 2023

#### Author(s)
Nathan Collier  
Bill Toulas  
Daniel Milisic

enhanced.Root cause: The malware infestation on the T95 TV box, primarily caused by pre-installed malicious software, specifically the DGBLauncher app, acted as the APK loader for the Corejava classes.dex file. The device had root access enabled, further exacerbating the security risks. *The T95 TV box, available on Amazon and AliExpress for as low as $40, came with sophisticated malware embedded in its firmware* (https://securityaffairs.com/140866/security/t95-android-tv-box-malware.html). *The device's ROM was signed with test keys and named 'Walleye' after the Google Pixel 2* (https://github.com/DesktopECHO/T95-H616-Malware). *The T95 TV box utilized an AllWinner T616 processor and ran on Android 10 OS* (https://hackread.com/amazon-android-tv-box-malware/).
enhanced.Organization/industry/location: The blog does not specify an organization or industry but indicates that the affected devices were available on Amazon.
enhanced.Start date \u2013 End date: The analysis was reported on January 30, 2023. The exact start and end dates of the malware presence are not specified.
MITRE TTPs: T1071.001 Application Layer Protocol: Web Protocols
T1556.001 Modify Authentication Process: Re-enable root access
T1059.007 Command and Scripting Interpreter: JavaScript
T1070.006 Indicator Removal on Host: Timestomp
enhanced.Impact: The number of affected devices or financial losses is not specified in the document. However, the malware caused significant security risks, including unauthorized internet traffic and potential data theft. *The malware resembles 'CopyCat,' an Android malware strain previously seen in adware campaigns* (https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/android-tv-box-on-amazon-came-pre-installed-with-malware/). *The malware was constantly trying to find a C2 server to upload telemetry data* (https://github.com/DesktopECHO/T95-H616-Malware). *Additionally, Adups malware was also identified on the device* (https://hackread.com/amazon-android-tv-box-malware/).
Mitigation: Perform a factory reset of the T95 TV box to remove any potentially downloaded malware.
Remove the pre-installed DGBLauncher app using the adb command:
Install a secure TV launcher to replace DGBLauncher.
Remove the Corejava directory and prevent its recreation using the following commands:
*Additionally, set up Pi-hole to monitor and block malicious traffic* (https://github.com/DesktopECHO/T95-H616-Malware).

Detection Signature.Port: N/A (adb connection is usually over USB)
Internal checks: Setting1: Ensure no root access toggle is present in settings.
Setting2: Verify no unexpected directories like /data/system/Corejava exist.
Setting3: Ensure no unexpected applications like DGBLauncher are installed.
External scanning: Monitor network traffic for unusual patterns, specifically connections to known malicious URLs such as hxxps://dy.kr.wildpettykiwi.info/dykr/update.

IoCs: Malicious Launcher APK Package Name: com.swe.dgbluancher
Additional Information: *Daniel Milisic, a Canadian systems security consultant, discovered the malware and created a script to nullify its payload* (https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/android-tv-box-on-amazon-came-pre-installed-with-malware/).

*The device was initially purchased to run the Pi-hole DNS sinkhole to protect against unwanted content* (https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/android-tv-box-on-amazon-came-pre-installed-with-malware/).
*The malware used a command and control server at adc.flyermobi.com, which has since been taken offline* (https://github.com/DesktopECHO/T95-H616-Malware).
*Milisic used tcpflow and nethogs to monitor traffic and trace malware* (https://securityaffairs.com/140866/security/t95-android-tv-box-malware.html).

title: Recent TZW Campaigns Revealed As Part of GlobeImposter Malware Family
content:
#### Description
Since 2017, campaigns delivering GlobeImposter have continued to proliferate even though the ransomware has only evolved slightly. GlobeImposter is most often delivered via phishing email as an attachment or a link to a malicious attachment. The payloads are typically distributed via 7zip or traditional zip file archives. The archives often include a JavaScript (.js) file that downloads and executes the GlobeImposter payload.

More recent campaigns from within the past three years still tend to follow this formula.

GlobeImposter has also been distributed as a later-stage infection within some well-known botnets. For example, in 2017 GlobeImposter was distributed via the Necurs botnet. This occurred as part of multiple spam campaigns that also included 7zip archives and followed the execution flow previously described.

AhnLab’s research revealed a ransomware campaign they referred to as “TZW” with victims in South Korea. The name is derived from the first 3 characters of the TOR-based victim portal. A closer look suggests that “TZW” samples represent a new variant of the GlobeImposter family.

#### Reference URL(s)
1. https://www.sentinelone.com/blog/recent-tzw-campaigns-revealed-as-part-of-globeimposter-malware-family/

#### Publication Date
February 15, 2023

#### Author(s)
Jim Walter

enhanced.Incident: TZW Ransomware Campaigns Revealed As Part of GlobeImposter Malware Family
enhanced.Root cause: Misconfigured Apache server exposing a publicly viewable Apache Server Status Page, which revealed the active virtual hosts used for the ransomware campaigns.
enhanced.Threat Actor/group/campaign: GlobeImposter (also known as LOLNEK or LOLKEK)
enhanced.Start date \u2013 End date: Documented campaign in February 2023 (exact start and end dates not specified)
MITRE TTPs: T1027.002: Obfuscated Files or Information: Software Packing
T1547.001: Boot or Logon Autostart Execution: Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder
enhanced.Impact: Not explicitly stated in the blog, but the impact generally includes data encryption and potential data loss for the affected organizations.

Secure Apache Server Configuration: Disable the Apache Server Status Page or restrict it to internal access only.
Regularly review and update server configurations to minimize exposure.

Email Phishing Protection: Implement email filtering solutions to detect and block phishing emails containing malicious attachments or links.

Endpoint Protection: Deploy advanced endpoint protection solutions like SentinelOne Singularity™ to detect and prevent ransomware activities.
Configure the endpoint protection to automatically block and rollback malicious activities.

Backup and Recovery: Maintain regular offline backups of critical data.
Test the backup and recovery processes periodically to ensure data can be restored quickly in case of a ransomware attack.

User Training: Conduct regular training sessions for employees to recognize and report phishing attempts.

Internal checks: Setting1: Ensure Apache Server Status Page is disabled or restricted – In platform
Setting2: Ensure Apache Server configuration files do not expose sensitive URLs – Inside VMs
Setting3: Regular audit of Apache server security configurations – Inside VMs
External scanning: Publicly accessible Apache Server Status Page

enhanced.Additional Info: *ASEC analysis team discovered* (https://asec.ahnlab.com/en/46812/) the TZW ransomware campaign. The ransomware encrypts files adding the “TZW” extension and uses the “System Boot Info” disguise (*System Boot Info*). It is created in a .NET format and involves a loader file named 'GvsqHuTYODA.exe' (*created in a .NET format*; *GvsqHuTYODA.exe*) which registers in the task scheduler. *Deepwatch's collaboration with SentinelOne* (https://www.deepwatch.com/labs/cyber-intel-brief-feb-15-22-2023/) reveals that TZW ransomware uses the same infrastructure to host TOR websites. Additionally, *GoDaddy disclosed a multi-year cyber attack campaign* (https://www.deepwatch.com/labs/cyber-intel-brief-feb-15-22-2023/) impacting up to 1.2 million customers.
